name: Ye'kwana
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: Une étude instrumentale permet en fait de constater qu'il existe deux phénomènes prosodiques qui se superposent : l'allongement vocalique et l'accent tonal. [p. 87] … On observe une forte tendance parmi les mots de deux à cinq syllabes contenant uniquement une racine et des affixes —pas de clitiques— à présenter la plus haute valeur de F0 sur la voyelle de la pénultième syllabe. [p. 93] … Les mots de deux et trois syllabes présentent aussi une valeur de F0 plus élevée sur la voyelle de la pénultième syllabe, c'est-à-dire, la première syllabe des mots à deux syllabes et la deuxième voyelle des mots à trois syllabes. [p. 94]
new_statements.translation: An instrumental study in fact shows that there are two superimposed prosodic phenomena: vowel lengthening and tonal accent. [p. 87] … A strong tendency is observed among words of two to five syllables containing only a root and affixes — no clitics — to present the highest F0 value on the vowel of the penultimate syllable. [p. 93] … Words of two and three syllables also present a higher F0 value on the vowel of the penultimate syllable, i.e. the first syllable of two-syllable words and the second vowel of three-syllable words. [p. 94]
new_statements.citation: Cáceres, Natalia. 2011. Grammaire fonctionnelle-typologique du ye'kwana, langue caribe du Venezuela. Thèse de doctorat, Université Lumière Lyon 2 (NNT 2011LYO20089).
new_statements.locator: Ch. 2, §2.5 'Prosodie et accent', p. 87; §2.5.2 'Accentuation tonale', pp. 93-94 (PDF pp. 99, 105-106)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (476 pp., text layer; PDF page = thesis page + 12, checked). All three quoted sentences are verbatim: p. 87 (PDF 99) "Une étude instrumentale permet en fait de constater qu'il existe deux phénomènes prosodiques qui se superposent : l'allongement vocalique et l'accent tonal." (opening of §2.5 Prosodie et accent); p. 93 (PDF 105) "On observe une forte tendance parmi les mots de deux à cinq syllabes contenant uniquement une racine et des affixes —pas de clitiques— à présenter la plus haute valeur de F0 sur la voyelle de la pénultième syllabe."; p. 94 (PDF 106) "Les mots de deux et trois syllabes présentent aussi une valeur de F0 plus élevée sur la voyelle de la pénultième syllabe, c'est…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Two layers: (i) a word-level tonal accent realised as the F0 peak on the penultimate syllable of the (clitic-less) word; (ii) a rhythmic layer of quantity-sensitive iambic feet built left-to-right, whose light heads (even-numbered open syllables) are lengthened, heavy (closed/long) syllables being foot heads; the author treats the two as independent and, in 2018, says no primary-stress claim has been made and the iambic metrical system may be 'the closest the language gets to a stress system'.
new_statements.secondary_stress: The iambic lengthening pattern (CV.CVː)(CV.CVː)… is what earlier work (Hall, Chavier 1999, Cáceres 2007) called the accent; Cáceres 2018 p. 172 notes that in other Cariban languages iambic lengthening is treated as secondary stress but no such claim is made for Ye'kwana. Per 2011 the final syllable of 4+-syllable words is lengthened (so not extrametrical), trisyllables do not lengthen the final, and bisyllables show no rhythmic lengthening (their prominence is tonal, on the first syllable).
new_statements.exceptions: Words carrying clitics (=je, =komo): the F0 peak is not consistently on the penult of the clitic-inclusive word and sometimes falls on the penult of the stem excluding the clitic (pp. 94-95); author calls for more data with more speakers (sample: 47 tokens/20 words speaker 1 in a carrier sentence, 30 tokens/15 words speaker 2 in isolation).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (morphologically defined word: root + affixes, excluding clitics); acoustic F0 and duration measurements on elicited words in a carrier phrase and in isolation; Caura-basin variety, Venezuela.
new_statements.identity_note: Cáceres 2011/2018 describe the Ye'kwana of the Caura basin (Bolívar, Venezuela); Hall 1988 describes 'De'kwana' (Erebato / Upper Caura dialect; Cáceres 2011 p. 88 and passim notes dialectal differences, e.g. üwü 1st person); Costa's work concerns the Brazilian Auaris (Roraima) variety. Glottolog 5.1 lists no dialect-level codes under maqu1238 in the target record.

sources.note: §2.5 'Prosodie et accent' (pp. 87-96): instrumental study finds two superimposed prosodic phenomena — quantity-sensitive iambic rhythmic vowel lengthening built left-to-right (foot level) and a tonal accent (F0 peak) on the penultimate syllable of the word (words without clitics, 2-5 syllables); with clitics the F0 peak is not consistently on the penult; earlier authors (Hall, Chavier 1999, Cáceres 2007) had described the 'accent' as purely rhythmic every second syllable (iambic).

sources.citation: Cáceres Arandia, Natalia. 2018. Syllable Reduction in Ye'kwana: Morphologized Phonology. International Journal of American Linguistics 84(2): 159-205. doi:10.1086/696196
sources.note: §2.2.1.3 (pp. 170-172): iambic lengthening of light syllables, feet built from the left edge, last syllable extrametrical, no degenerate feet, heavy syllables always foot heads (citing Cáceres 2007:102-15); 'rythmic vowel lengthening does not seem to be correlated to any particular pitch pattern'; 'in Ye'kwana, there has not yet been a definite claim about another kind of stress... It might well be that the metric system is the closest the language gets to a stress system' (p. 172). §2.3 (pp. 180-181): syllable reduction and stress are independent.
